product: SUNLU PLA filament — Color: Black; Size: 1 kg
review:
Not so sure about this stuff - print issues

I'm using a Prusa I3. It's been a good printer so far, but I've been feeding it filament from Prusa. Recently I switched to this SUNLU black PLA, and I've seen issues.One is definitely the manufacturer's fault. The spool it comes on is a typical plastic bobbin. They put a small hole in the bobbin to thread the filament into, to hold the end in place while they wind it. Unfortunately the hole is on the inside of the cylinder instead of on the side, which means there's a tiny nub of filament sticking through the bobbin's inner ring - the thing it rotates on as filament gets drawn by the printer. Once a revolution, this tends to get caught on the printer's support rod, and the filament stepper motor then has to pull against the weight of the whole spool to get the next inch of PLA. I can't be sure because I wasn't watching it, but I think that's why a 10 hour print job failed partway through - the tension caused something to get misaligned and the printed model got knocked over.I tried cutting off the nub, but it's about impossible to get it all, so my workaround involves electrical tape over the nub, an extra tube between the support and the bobbin, and lithium grease. So far I think it's working, but witchcraft involving lithium grease shouldn't be necessaryThe other issue is that this stuff seems fussy about temperature. Printed at 215, it was messy and stringy. At 210 it's still prone to leaving threads all over the print job, but it's better. I never had this threads problem with Prusa's filament. Maybe it's a matter of tuning and experimenting but I can't say i'm satisfied. I'll note I also got some PETG translucent from SUNLU and it didn't have this stringing problem, but then PETG isn't PLA.Bottom line, I think I'll stick to Prusa's more expensive PLA in future, and do more with PETG, as it doesn't seem harder to print and seems to come out a bit better. I think I can finish my current project with this PLA, but I don't quite trust it. For people concerned about color, though, this is a nice rich deep black, with some gloss (where it doesn't string).Addendum: I had ongoing adhesion problems with this stuff. A model that printed fine with Prusa's house PLA filament would routinely come off the platter during printing with this stuff, and in the end I had to add extra material to the model's base, and print with a brim, to get it to work. I got a usable print in the end but it took half the spool to figure out how, after trying realigning the printer, cleaning the platter with acetone and alcohol before each attempt, etc. The loss of time is what decided it for me - there's not much more annoying than having a 6 hour print job fail after 3 hours, except for when it happens 3 times in a row.

Just keep it protected from humidity and it will treat you well!

product: SUNLU ABS filament — Color: 1000g Abs White; Size: 1kg
review:
Be careful of warpage and film stress

Overall, this material prints fairly well. However, it has definitely demonstrated a few pretty glaring differences from the other ABS I have used.Previously, I have only used Bambu Labs ABS material (I've just polished off my third roll since getting the printer 6 months ago). I ordered the Sunlu because I needed white for the specific application I was working on, and couldn't get the Bambu stuff fast enough.For reference, I use a "bed slinger" style of printer - specifically a Bambu Labs A1.The first thing I noticed was the lack of smell - the Bambu ABS definitely emits a "hot plastic" smell during processing (I use it in a closed, will ventilated room for exactly that reason).The second thing I noticed was my plate getting completely rotated around during the print! While the bed was moving forward and backward, apparently something caught on the nozzle hard enough to dislodge the plate.I cleaned off the plate and restarted the print. At about the same point in the process (layer height~4 mm), I started to hear loud scraping, so I stopped the process, and then noticed that the corners were lifting.  Not the corners of the print, but the corners of the PRINT PLATE! I didn't measure, but my estimate is that the corners showed a z-displacement of at least 3mm. The adhesion was terrific between the ABS and the plate, but the stress was pretty incredible.So I swapped back to my less-than-ideal, stinky Bambu ABS, and successfully completed the print.There is definitely a difference between the two, that makes the Sunlu material much more prone to warp , and thus less than ideal for large-footprint modelsSo much for the idea that Sunlu and Bambu filament are the same manufacturer with different labels. That might be true for the PLA or PETG, but definitely not due the ABS.I was always confused when people complained about how hard it was to print ABS - now I understand.

The print released itself from the bed after cooling to roughly 70*C. Simply lifted it off the plate and removed the brim. I'll definitely be ordering more!

Reliable PLA+ with good strength and clean prints, minor diameter inconsistency noted

This SUNLU PLA Plus in black has been a solid workhouse filament for my 3D printing projects. PLA+ delivers noticeably better impact resistance and flexibility compared to standard PLA, which matters for functional parts and anything that needs to hold up to some stress. The prints have good layer adhesion and the surfaces come out smooth without requiring excessive fine-tuning of settings.The neatly wound spool claim checks out. It was a small issue that most experienced printers would handle easily by pausing and letting it catch up, but worth noting. For the price versus performance ratio, this is still a strong value and I have had far worse issues with other brands at similar prices. A reliable everyday PLA+ that I would recommend.

product: SUNLU PLA Phosphorus filament — Color: White (Glow Green); Size: 1 kg
review:
Spool design bad across multiple revisions. Filament itself is great.

The filament itself is great, but the spools are consistently troublesome. The old spool had a not on the outer rim that didn't play well with the Bambu AMS. No big deal, I run a lot of glow filament which will eat up the AMS anyways, but the notch prevented me from using other materials. They recently updated their spool to be compatible with the AMS. Great, I thought. Then I received a new spool and wasted half a kilo on prints that failed due to design changes in the spool. They got rid of the rim notch which is good, but also got rid of the bevel on the cutouts on the sides of the spool, which is very bad. The lack of a bevel caused the spool to hang up on the filament hanger on the back of my P1P.After the first failed print, I pulled the spool off and verified there were no tangles, put it back on and ran a shorter test print. No issue. Ran another bigger print and it failed horribly. Pulled it back off and thoroughly inspected it, then tried running again while sitting there watching it. The hard angle on the edges of the cutouts were hanging up on the base of the spool hanger. It jumped over it and would feed again past the next hole until the spool worked itself close enough to the back of the printer to drag against it and hang up again. It causes feed issues, ghost layers, and broken filament.Rigging up a solution currently. Will see if it works. Either way. They need to get their spool design dialed in. I don't want to have to respool filament that's already on a reusable spool.

product: ELEGOO PC filament — Color: Pc Filament Black 1000g; Size: 1KG
review:
String theory

I’m most interested in functional prints so I immediately gravitate towards the strongest filaments, and polycarbonate is well known to be one of the strongest plastics in existence, being used for things like bulletproof windows in banks. It’s also really pretty when properly printed. I’m still learning and dialing in my slicer settings, but here’s what seems to work. I dried the spool for a good 12 hours at 75c, straight from the vacuum pack into the dryer. PC is super viscous so a .6mm nozzle really helps. Use the textured build plate that came with your printer and a thin skim of glue, and print at the lowest possible temp, which in my case is 263c (3 above recommended minimum) and 100c on the bed. Turn your print and travel speeds way down.  Adhesion is good with this stuff and I didn’t have much in the way of issues with the first layer. The problem with this stuff is that even with a properly dried fresh spool, a dryer, and my desert climate it likes to string. Printing at the lowest possible temp and turning your print speeds down helps, but the issue is gradual buildup on the outside of the nozzle every time it crosses a string. Eventually this turns into a big booger that may or may not damage your print. On one test run said booger got caught in a couple wall loops and dragged them off the print causing a blemish. I’ve gone so far as to manually remove the buildup with tweezers mid print, and with 100% infill and ironing of all solid layers, this means many trips to the printer over many hours to check the nozzle. I’m going to start treating my nozzle with PTFE paint and double check the nozzle height, and just maybe I’ll be able to run an 18 hour print without having to clean off the buildup.Now the good. Polycarbonate is one of the strongest plastics in existence. It boasts incredible impact and heat resistance and also takes a beautiful polish. It’s lacking in the UV and chemical resistance departments though so if you’re making a part that will be exposed to the elements or harsh solvents go with ASA or nylon respectively. Neither look nearly as good. A clean polycarbonate print comes out super shiny and resembles a brand new vinyl record. The last nice thing about this filament is the price at about half what reinforced nylon costs, and since I happen to have a centauri carbon printer I get to stay entirely OEM with this stuff. And I’m just getting started.

review:
Incredible surface finish. MUST USE SPECIFIC NOZZLE!

I love this stuff, the surface finish comes out so premium on all my prints. My girlfriend said "that doesn't even look like a 3d print" because the surface finish is so good. I have got like 6 rolls in the last two months. FIRE!Update: This stuff continues to be my absolute favorite filament. I am now selling production products using it because the surface finish is so excellent. I have learned a few things after printing about 40 rolls of it. The first thing, you must dry it. If you have a dryer that goes to 55c thats fine but dry it at 55c for at least 24hrs. I print it straight from the dryer. If you have a 70c dryer, thats even better. I would recommend the 70c SUNLU dryer.The next thing is slicer settings. It is very similar to Bambu PETG-CF, so I typically just use that preset, and the only thing I change is setting fan pre start time to 2 seconds. This helps with overhangs.The last thing is nozzle clumping. PETG-CF is pretty sticky, and likes to build up on the nozzle over time. Eventually it will build up enough that a blob deposits on your print. I tried a ton of solutions to prevent this such as non stick nozzles, plastic repellent paint, and different nozzle geometries. In the end, what I found worked best was to just simply use an OEM Bambu Hardened Steel Nozzle. It MUST be the quick change nozzle for the A and H series printer. The old nozzle for X1C, P1P, and P1S will blob no matter what you do. Do not use aftermarket nozzles, all the ones I tried blob. Just please use the OEM bambu quick change nozzle. It has a steep angled tip which sits back far away from the print surface and will not allow plastic to build up on it's edges.Happy printing and mark this review as helpful if you learned something!

This TPU material is super grippy, and doesn't slide off anything easily, even when it's TPU on nylon polymer composite plastic. The bed adhesion on my build plate was fantastic, and the final prints feel structurally solid without any delamination under mechanical stress.Tangle-Free Spooling: The filament is wound cleanly on the spool. I experienced no snags, binding, or overlapping tension issues while the extruder pulled it from the external roller.If your engineering projects require functional flexibility and you have your direct drive extrusion profile dialed in, this is a highly capable and predictable filament that produces excellent modifiable parts.

Making great headbases for my fursuits and all, but the last two rolls I will get maybe a 3rd of the way through a print and it has these kinks in it that don’t let it go through an extruder. My last 8 prints have been fails due to this, and I’m getting to the point I am afraid to try another. If it worked well, I’d love it until the end but I think I will be looking into a different brand. If you can get a roll that doesn’t have kinks in it, this is a great fit for you. The adhesion is great, it feels durable if you print with a high enough infill (layers occasionally rip), and it’s a good deal on it. But I think it might be beneficial seeking elsewhere especially if you have larger TPU prints you are making.
